1 December 2026

questions.subtopic: UN Charter: prohibition on use of force
questions.stem: Under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which conduct must Member States generally refrain from in their international relations?
options: Threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state
Any economic sanction approved by a regional organisation
All criticism of another state's domestic policy
Any diplomatic negotiation involving a disputed border
explanations: Correct. Article 2(4) requires Members to refrain from the threat or use of force against a state's territorial integrity or political independence, or otherwise inconsistently with UN purposes.
The Charter does not prohibit every economic sanction; sanctions may be authorised under Chapter VII.
Political criticism is not, by itself, the threat or use of force addressed by Article 2(4).
Negotiation over a disputed border is not prohibited; peaceful settlement is encouraged.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: International Relations and Events; Charter of the United Nations, Article 2(4), full text; https://www.un.org/en/about-us/un-charter/full-text

questions.subtopic: International Court of Justice: contentious jurisdiction
questions.stem: Two states submit a contentious dispute to the International Court of Justice. Which statement best describes the legal basis of the Court's jurisdiction in such a case?
options: The Court has compulsory jurisdiction over every dispute between UN members
Jurisdiction generally depends on the consent of the states concerned
The UN General Assembly must approve every judgment before it becomes binding
Any private company may independently file a contentious case against a state
explanations: ICJ jurisdiction is not automatically compulsory for every dispute between all UN members.
Correct. In contentious cases, the Court's jurisdiction rests on state consent, which may be expressed through a special agreement, treaty clause or optional-clause declarations.
The General Assembly does not approve ICJ judgments; judgments in contentious cases bind the parties to that case.
Private companies are not parties entitled to institute contentious proceedings before the ICJ.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: International Relations and Events; Statute of the International Court of Justice, Articles 34–36; https://www.icj-cij.org/statute

questions.subtopic: Photoelectric effect: intensity and kinetic energy
questions.stem: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold frequency shines on a clean metal surface. If only the light intensity is increased, what happens in the ideal photoelectric-effect model?
options: Maximum kinetic energy increases, but the number of emitted electrons stays fixed
Maximum kinetic energy remains fixed, while the emission rate can increase
Threshold frequency decreases
Work function of the metal increases
explanations: At fixed frequency, increasing intensity does not increase the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons.
Correct. Greater intensity supplies more photons per unit time, so the photoelectron emission rate can increase, while maximum kinetic energy remains set by frequency.
Threshold frequency is a material property determined by work function; intensity does not lower it.
The work function is a property of the metal surface and is not increased merely by changing incident intensity.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: General Science; India’s Achievements in Science and Technology; NCERT Physics, Class XII, Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter, Einstein photoelectric equation; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction that has already reached equilibrium at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: The equilibrium constant increases
The equilibrium composition shifts towards products
The forward and reverse reactions reach equilibrium faster, but the equilibrium constant is unchanged
The catalyst changes the enthalpy of reaction
explanations: A catalyst does not alter the thermodynamic equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.
A catalyst accelerates both directions; it does not shift the equilibrium composition by itself.
Correct. By lowering activation barriers for forward and reverse pathways, a catalyst helps the system attain equilibrium faster without changing K.
A catalyst changes reaction rates, not the reaction enthalpy of the initial and final states.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: General Science; India’s Achievements in Science and Technology; NCERT Chemistry, Class XII, Chemical Kinetics and Catalysis; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: Why can chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) cause catalytic depletion of stratospheric ozone after reaching the upper atmosphere?
options: They release chlorine radicals under ultraviolet radiation, and those radicals can participate in repeated ozone-destroying cycles
They convert all atmospheric oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
They absorb only infrared radiation and therefore cool the stratosphere
They increase the rate of nitrogen fixation in the stratosphere
explanations: Correct. UV photolysis of CFCs can release chlorine radicals; catalytic cycles allow a chlorine radical to destroy many ozone molecules before being deactivated.
CFC photochemistry does not convert atmospheric oxygen into carbon dioxide.
CFC-driven ozone depletion is not explained by infrared absorption cooling the stratosphere.
Nitrogen fixation is not the mechanism of CFC-related ozone loss.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Environmental issues; Disaster Management – Prevention and Mitigation Strategies; UNEP, Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion; Montreal Protocol background; https://ozone.unep.org/science/assessment

questions.stem: Under India's Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, which set of streams is used for source segregation by waste generators?
options: Wet waste, dry waste and domestic hazardous waste
Only recyclable and non-recyclable waste
Biomedical waste, e-waste and radioactive waste in one household bin
Compost, sewage and construction debris
explanations: Correct. The 2016 Rules require segregation into biodegradable/wet waste, non-biodegradable/dry waste and domestic hazardous waste.
The Rules specify a separate domestic hazardous stream in addition to wet and dry waste.
Biomedical, e-waste and radioactive waste are governed by separate rules and should not be combined as one household stream.
Compost is generally a treatment product, sewage is a wastewater stream, and construction debris has separate management provisions.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Environmental issues; Disaster Management – Prevention and Mitigation Strategies; Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; https://moef.gov.in/

questions.stem: A government's fiscal deficit is ₹8.4 lakh crore and its interest payments are ₹2.1 lakh crore. What is the primary deficit?
options: ₹6.3 lakh crore
₹8.4 lakh crore
₹10.5 lakh crore
₹4.2 lakh crore
explanations: Correct. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 8.4 − 2.1 = ₹6.3 lakh crore.
₹8.4 lakh crore is the fiscal deficit before removing interest payments.
Adding interest payments would not produce the primary deficit.
₹4.2 lakh crore is not obtained from the stated definition.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Economic and Social Development of India and Telangana; Government of India, Union Budget glossary / public-finance definitions; https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/

questions.stem: A taxable supply is consumed in State B, although the supplier is located in State A. Which principle best explains why GST is described as a destination-based consumption tax?
options: Tax revenue is assigned only to the state where the supplier's factory is located
Tax is intended to accrue to the place of consumption, subject to the applicable inter-State settlement rules
GST is levied only when goods cross an international border
The tax is collected exclusively by local municipal bodies
explanations: The supplier's location alone is not the defining destination principle.
Correct. GST follows the destination principle: the tax burden/revenue is associated with consumption, with IGST settlement rules governing inter-State supplies.
GST applies to domestic supplies as well as imports; it is not limited to international borders.
GST is administered through the Union and State tax framework, not exclusively by municipalities.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Economic and Social Development of India and Telangana; GST Council, GST structure and destination-based taxation; https://gstcouncil.gov.in/

questions.stem: Which feature characterises the Bhabar belt along the Himalayan foothills?
options: Fine alluvium deposited in a deltaic estuary
A porous belt of coarse pebbles and sediments in which streams may disappear underground
A permanently waterlogged marsh belt south of the Terai
A high-altitude zone of glacial cirques
explanations: A deltaic estuary is not the Bhabar belt.
Correct. The Bhabar is a narrow, coarse, porous depositional belt at the foothills where streams can sink into the permeable deposits.
The marshy belt where streams re-emerge is the Terai, not Bhabar.
Glacial cirques are high-mountain landforms, not the foothill Bhabar belt.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Physical, Social and Economic Geography of India; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Physiographic divisions of the Northern Plains; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: Which comparison between the Eastern Ghats and Western Ghats is geographically most accurate?
options: Both ranges form equally continuous escarpments along the coast
The Eastern Ghats are more discontinuous because major east-flowing rivers dissect them, whereas the Western Ghats are comparatively continuous
The Western Ghats are lower and more discontinuous than the Eastern Ghats throughout their length
The Eastern Ghats are a young fold mountain system formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
explanations: The two ranges do not have equal continuity; the Eastern Ghats are notably discontinuous.
Correct. Large rivers such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri cut across the Eastern Ghats, while the Western Ghats form a more continuous escarpment.
This reverses the usual continuity comparison and is not accurate as a general description.
The Eastern Ghats are an ancient eroded range, not a young Himalayan-style fold system.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Physical, Social and Economic Geography of India; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Peninsular Plateau and Western/Eastern Ghats; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: By what name is the Brahmaputra generally known when it enters India in Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet?
options: Teesta
Siang or Dihang
Subansiri
Lohit
explanations: Teesta is a separate Himalayan river system.
Correct. The Yarlung Tsangpo enters Arunachal Pradesh and is known as the Siang or Dihang before major tributaries join it.
Subansiri is a major tributary that joins the Brahmaputra system in Assam.
Lohit is another important tributary, not the name used for the main river at its entry into Arunachal Pradesh.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Physical, Social and Economic Geography of India; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Himalayan river systems; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: The Ghadar Party was organised in 1913 by Indian expatriate revolutionaries. In which city was its early headquarters and newspaper activity centred?
options: London
San Francisco
Berlin
Tokyo
explanations: London hosted several Indian nationalist activities, but it was not the Ghadar Party's principal early centre.
Correct. The Ghadar movement developed among Indian migrants on the Pacific Coast, with its headquarters and newspaper activity centred in San Francisco.
Berlin was associated with the Berlin Committee/Indian Independence Committee, a distinct wartime initiative.
Tokyo was not the Ghadar Party's principal early headquarters.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Socio-economic, Political and Cultural History of Modern India with special emphasis on Indian National Movement; standard reference: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ghadar movement chapter; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: What was the central issue behind the controversy over the Ilbert Bill of 1883 in British India?
options: It proposed elected Indian members for the Viceroy's Executive Council
It sought to remove the racial bar preventing qualified Indian judges from trying European British subjects in criminal cases
It introduced separate electorates for religious communities
It transferred control of the Indian Army to provincial legislatures
explanations: The Bill did not propose elected Indian membership in the Viceroy's Executive Council.
Correct. The Bill sought to allow senior Indian magistrates and judges to try European British subjects, provoking strong opposition from the European community.
Separate electorates were associated with the 1909 reforms, not the Ilbert Bill.
The Bill did not transfer military control to provincial legislatures.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Socio-economic, Political and Cultural History of Modern India with special emphasis on Indian National Movement; standard reference: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, colonial legal reforms; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

questions.stem: Which limited parliamentary function was introduced by the Indian Councils Act, 1892?
options: Members could discuss the annual budget and ask questions subject to restrictions, but could not vote on the budget
Members could remove the Viceroy through a no-confidence motion
Provincial legislatures received full responsible government
The Act established universal adult franchise
explanations: Correct. The 1892 Act expanded legislative councils and permitted limited discussion of the budget and questions, without granting a vote on the budget.
A no-confidence mechanism to remove the Viceroy was not created by the Act.
Full provincial responsible government came much later, notably under the 1935 Act's provincial autonomy provisions.
Universal adult franchise was not introduced by the 1892 Act.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Socio-economic, Political and Cultural History of Modern India with special emphasis on Indian National Movement; Indian Councils Act, 1892, statutory text and standard modern-history references; https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/Vict/55-56/14/contents
